verdict.rationale: DBOS runs as a library inside your own application, backed by your Postgres, with no separate orchestration server. A DBOS-managed Conductor can act as the control plane: it detects interrupted workflows, recovers them to healthy executors, and lets you pause, restart or fork workflows. That matches the hybrid split of your workers plus a vendor-managed control plane. However, the evidence never states that application code and workflow data stay inside your network when the managed Conductor is used. missing for 10: explicit documentation of the data boundary and network connectivity model between self-run executors and DBOS-managed Conductor, security/privacy guarantees that workflow inputs and outputs are not sent to the vendor, independent hands-on corroboration of the hybrid deployment.

support.subject: As a platform engineer, I run workers in my own infrastructure while the vendor manages the orchestration control plane — code and data stay inside my network

citations.quote: The open-source DBOS library uses Postgres to orchestrate durable workflows and queues. There's no separate orchestration server and no infrastructure required besides Postgres.
Conductor automatically detects when a workflow is interrupted (for example, if its executor disconnects or crashes) and recovers the workflow to another healthy executor.
It manages workflows, queues, schedules, applications, and API keys against DBOS-managed Conductor or a self-hosted Conductor
From the Conductor dashboard, you can pause any workflow execution, start any stopped or enqueued workflow, or restart any workflow from a specific step.
